messages.author: 8156fdd09adbc581
messages.subject: Poisson vs. negative binomial
parts:
Hello,
I am trying to determine if I should use a Poisson or a negative
binomial model. What indicator should I use to determine if my data
is overdispersed? Does unmarked have a built-in method of determining
if the negative binomial is appropriate? For instance, these are the
results from the best-fit negative binomial model I have run on my
data so far. What exactly does the non-significant z-score tell me?
Appreciate any help.

pcount(formula = ~maj_prey + area_am_riv + block2 + block3 +
block4 ~ shape_am + pladj, data = tigerUMF, K = 22, mixture =
c("NB"))

Abundance:
Estimate SE z P(>|z|)
(Intercept) 1.746 0.305 5.72 1.05e-08
shape_am 0.867 0.210 4.13 3.65e-05
pladj 0.906 0.240 3.78 1.58e-04

Detection:
Estimate SE z P(>|z|)
(Intercept) -3.634 0.351 -10.34 4.55e-25
maj_prey 0.317 0.128 2.48 1.33e-02
area_am_riv -0.779 0.172 -4.53 5.88e-06
block2 -0.375 0.328 -1.14 2.53e-01
block3 -1.019 0.368 -2.77 5.61e-03
block4 -1.828 0.373 -4.90 9.56e-07

Dispersion:
Estimate SE z P(>|z|)
10.5 68.2 0.154 0.877

AIC: 861.418

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Poisson vs. negative binomial
parts:
hi Neil,

people would normally look at the AIC from a model that assumes a Poisson and that which assumes a NB and choose that distribution which gives clearly a lower AIC (for instance, more than 2 AIC units); see for instance our early Nmix paper in Ecol.Appl. (Kery et al. 2005). Typically, the NB turns out to be favoured by AIC. Be aware that the NB can produce very high and sometimes unrealistic abundance estimates. If that happens, I would choose the Poisson. There is a paper on those unrealistic NB abundance estimates, about 2009 or 2010 somewhere in EcolApps or perhaps ConsBiol.

Regards -- Marc

Modeling Abundance Using N-Mixture Models: The Importance of Considering Ecological Mechanisms

Ecological Applications , Vol. 19, No. 3 (Apr., 2009), pp. 631-642


Kristen
